title: Prefill/Decode Handoff Protocol and Jitter Smoothing
creator: Lydia Chen
description:
Background: We continue to see SLO violations caused by small, sporadic bursts of long tail latency during continuous batching. Root analysis shows a combination of: (1) jittery admission of prefill requests that creates transient tiny batches at decode time, (2) suboptimal kernel selection for mixed sequence lengths when a handoff from prefill->decode occurs, and (3) contention spikes when kernel probing happens mid-decode. Goal: Reduce 99.9th token latency by 25-40% on mixed short/long workloads while keeping average cost per token within 5% of baseline. Success metrics: 99.9p token latency, p95/p99 request latency, fraction of decode handoffs that trigger kernel reprobe, and token-cost delta.

Proposed approach: Introduce an explicit prefill->decode handoff protocol combined with a lightweight jitter-smoothing admission layer.

1) Handoff protocol: when a prefill transitions to decode, attach a small metadata token (handoff hints) that includes: estimated remaining length, approximate kv-cache size, and a short compatibility fingerprint of the kernel path used during prefill. The decode scheduler will use this fingerprint to prefer compatible kernels or trigger a fast compatibility check rather than a full kernel reprobe.

2) Jitter-smoothing admission: implement a short, adaptive hold-window (2-12ms depending on load percentile) for tiny prefill batches. The window is jittered deterministically per-customer to avoid synchronized releases across tenants. The hold-window is latency-aware: under high tail pressure the window increases slightly to allow coalescing; under idle conditions it collapses to zero.

3) Kernel affinity ranking: add a lightweight ranking layer that scores candidate kernels for a decode based on: compatibility fingerprint, recent latency history for the model/seqlen bucket, and current GPU utilization. The ranking returns the top N candidate kernels so the scheduler can attempt fast fallback rather than a full probe.

4) Fast reprobe path: for cases where kernel fallback fails, implement a time-bounded reprobe that executes on a background stream and only blocks decode if there is a measurable win predicted (heuristic based on token budget and remaining sequence length).

Design notes: Keep the handoff hint size tiny (<=64 bytes) to avoid networking overhead. The hold-window must be tenant-aware so premium customers can opt-out (or get a lower window) to preserve latency SLAs. Kernel ranking should be cacheable keyed by model-version:seqlen-range:gpu-arch.

Rollout plan: Feature-flag the jitter-smoothing admission and handoff hints independently. Stage 1 (canary): enable on 5% of production traffic of internal staging customers and synthetic mixed workloads. Stage 2: expand to 25% with telemetry dashboards. Stage 3: enable globally with opt-outs for dedicated tenants.

Telemetry/observability: New metrics to emit: handoff_hint_rate, handoff_compatibility_match_rate, jitter_hold_time_ms (histogram), kernel_rank_choice, fast_reprobe_invocations, and decode_block_fraction. Add tracing spans for handoff serialization, ranking decision, and reprobe window.

Risks and mitigations: 1) Incorrect fingerprints could cause repeated fallback; mitigate by conservative fingerprinting and gradual rollout. 2) Hold-window could increase median latency for a subset of requests; mitigate by making window adaptive and tenant-aware. 3) Complexity in kernel ranking may mask underlying performance regressions; mitigate with canary and kill-switch.

Open questions: - What exact fingerprint bits are available cheaply from the runtime? (Luca to confirm). - Conservative defaults for hold-window sizing across instance types. - How to expose opt-out/priority per-customer at the routing layer?

Deliverables: design doc (Confluence link), feature flags, kernel ranking service, telemetry dashboards, e2e test harness and canary plan.
